query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy, exposure to high-temperature service leads to subtle, nanoscale grain-boundary segregation of specific alloying elements that are prone to diffuse faster along grain boundaries. This segregation triggers local compositional fluctuations that weaken the cohesive strength of grain boundaries and promote brittle intergranular fracture, distinctly diverging from the conventional precipitation-driven embrittlement seen in traditional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy with a compositionally complex matrix and no significant pre-existing grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic particles.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to a controlled high-temperature annealing treatment that simulates prolonged service conditions, while comparing with a control group maintained at baseline temperature.
generation.conditions: High-temperature annealing at service-relevant temperatures under uniaxial loading conditions. The test should cover a range of temperatures modestly above baseline to activate grain-boundary diffusion but below full phase transformation temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale grain-boundary segregation of select alloying elements that preferentially migrate under high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: The segregation of specific elements reduces the local grain-boundary cohesion and, by causing chemical inhomogeneities, leads to early crack initiation and brittle intergranular fracture. This mechanism is distinct because, unlike conventional alloys where brittle behavior is driven by coarse grain-boundary precipitates, here the critical change is subtle segregation without the formation of overt, large-scale precipitates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, annealed samples will show measurable reductions in toughness properties (e.g., lower fracture strain and increased brittle fracture features) correlated with localized compositional changes at grain boundaries, as observed by high-resolution microscopy and chemical analysis of grain boundaries.
generation.baseline: The initially homogeneous, single-phase microstructure with uniformly distributed alloying elements, which provides high fracture toughness and ductility.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys designed for tough, high-temperature applications; however, its relevance is bounded by service conditions that are sufficiently high to promote grain-boundary diffusion but not so high as to induce complete phase transformation or large-scale coarsening.
generation.uncertainty: The precise identity of the elements that segregate and the quantitative extent of segregation required to cause brittle behavior is uncertain. Additionally, the threshold temperature and loading conditions under which ductility loss becomes significant have not been fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same high-entropy alloy. Subject one set to high-temperature annealing under controlled conditions (stress-assisted if necessary) while maintaining the second set at room temperature as a baseline. Conduct post-treatment characterizations using transmission electron microscopy (for nanoscale grain-boundary structure) and atom probe tomography (for local chemistry) to detect any grain-boundary segregation. Perform mechanical tests (tensile or fracture toughness tests) to compare the onset and propagation of brittle fracture between the two groups.
measurements: Grain-boundary compositional profiles (via atom probe tomography or energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy)
Fracture toughness and strain-to-failure from mechanical testing
Fractographic analysis to identify intergranular fracture characteristics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not display statistically significant grain-boundary segregation or if their mechanical performance (fracture toughness and ductility) remains indistinguishable from the baseline samples, then the hypothesis—that nanoscale grain-boundary segregation causes brittle failure in high-entropy alloys—would be falsified.
